title: Cloud Database Architecture & Migration
description: I designed and maintained Essential Skills' cloud persistence architecture beginning with the 2011 migration of Hydra-Gen into a WebStart/cloud model. AWS SimpleDB became the long-running production core because it delivered very low operating cost, fast access and effectively maintenance-free scaling for our workload, even at roughly 80,000 monthly users. Over the years I repeatedly evaluated and implemented alternatives including DynamoDB, Aurora MySQL, RDS MySQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Azure Cosmos DB and Google Cloud options, while also building backup, migration and multi-cloud contingency tooling in Python.

sections.title: Hydra-Gen Cloud Migration
paragraphs: The original reason for adopting AWS persistence was to move Hydra-Gen into a WebStart/cloud deployment model around 2011.
SimpleDB became the central production database for the cloud generation of Essential Skills applications.

sections.title: SimpleDB Production Core
paragraphs: SimpleDB stored the major operational data used by the Essential Skills platform.

sections.title: Cost & Scale
paragraphs: One of the reasons SimpleDB remained in production for so long was its unusually strong cost/performance fit for our workload.
Even when the platform was serving roughly 80,000 monthly users, the core SimpleDB cost was typically only about $20–$40 per month while requiring essentially no manual scaling administration.

sections.title: SimpleDB Domain Design
paragraphs: I deliberately organized SimpleDB domains similarly to relational tables even though AWS guidance often encouraged a less structured approach.
The service had relatively small domain-size limits at the time, and separating concepts into clear logical domains made the system easier to manage and optimize.

sections.title: Logical Data Separation
paragraphs: I also separated major product and business concerns into different logical areas and, where useful, separate AWS organizational/account structures.

sections.title: Manual Join Optimization
paragraphs: SimpleDB did not provide relational joins, so the application layer handled cross-domain relationships.
I designed the data access around that limitation rather than performing many small dependent queries.
items: Creating correlation domains for frequently requested summaries

sections.title: Correlation & Reporting Domains
paragraphs: For expensive cross-domain reporting, I created purpose-specific domains containing already-correlated data.
For example, district-wide summaries could be generated without repeatedly traversing every school, program and student record at report time.

sections.title: Large Data via S3
paragraphs: When individual records required data too large or unsuitable for SimpleDB attributes, I stored the larger payload in Amazon S3 and kept only the reference in SimpleDB.
This provided a practical BLOB-style pattern without forcing oversized content into the database.

sections.title: Batch Operations
paragraphs: Wherever possible I used batch operations to reduce network overhead and improve throughput for bulk reads and writes.

sections.title: Version 5 to Version 6 Persistence
paragraphs: Hydra-Gen / Version 5 used the SmartDB/Rosetta persistence abstraction.

For Version 6 I built a new persistence layer focused specifically on SimpleDB while retaining compatibility with the same underlying production data, allowing both platform generations to operate during the migration.

sections.title: Maintaining an Unsupported SDK
paragraphs: When AWS required Elastic Beanstalk applications to move away from PHP 5, the existing SimpleDB SDK was no longer maintained for the newer environment.
Rather than abandon a stable production database, I updated the SimpleDB SDK myself so the applications could continue operating on the newer Beanstalk runtime.

sections.title: DynamoDB
paragraphs: I used DynamoDB both as a production database for newer systems and as an extension to the SimpleDB architecture.
items: Newer side systems where DynamoDB fit naturally

sections.title: Version 7 / Aurora MySQL
paragraphs: Version 7 initially used Amazon Aurora MySQL as a serious attempt to create a future migration path away from SimpleDB.
I designed and administered the Version 7 application database and ran Aurora in production for several years.

sections.title: Retiring Aurora
paragraphs: I adopted Aurora while the service was still relatively early and found that its rapid operational changes created too much maintenance overhead for our small team.
After repeatedly adapting to service changes, I retired Aurora rather than continue investing in a database that was not delivering enough practical advantage over the simpler alternatives.

sections.title: RDS MySQL Evaluation
paragraphs: I also evaluated standard Amazon RDS MySQL before selecting Aurora for the Version 7 relational database work.

sections.title: S3 / JSON Persistence
paragraphs: Version 7 also includes a working S3/JSON persistence mode inspired by the partitioning concepts used in the earlier ISAM architecture.
Schools, teachers, students and custom assignment data can be organized into hierarchical JSON objects/folders in S3.

sections.title: Hybrid Version 7 Persistence
paragraphs: The S3/JSON path currently works alongside DynamoDB rather than existing only as a theoretical alternative.
Different persistence mechanisms are used where each fits the data and operational needs best.

sections.title: MongoDB
paragraphs: I used MongoDB for selected lower-risk internal data in the Customer Operations platform, including quote-related data and internal messaging linked to customer records.
Authoritative school and student data remained in SimpleDB rather than being moved into MongoDB.

sections.title: Azure Disaster-Recovery Migration
paragraphs: In 2018 I built a functioning Azure contingency environment as a vendor-exit and disaster-recovery option.
I cloned the AWS EC2 application environment onto Azure Virtual Machines and wrote Python migration tooling to move SimpleDB data into Azure Cosmos DB.

sections.title: Azure Staging Validation
paragraphs: The staging software ran successfully against the Azure environment after migration.
The Azure/Cosmos configuration remained a fallback rather than becoming the primary platform because my testing found it slower and more expensive than the existing AWS/SimpleDB architecture.

sections.title: Google Cloud Migration Research
paragraphs: I also investigated Google Cloud as another vendor-exit path around 2018.
I prototyped a migration approach using Google's managed NoSQL services, but the effort did not reach the same level of completeness as the Azure contingency environment.

sections.title: Cassandra Evaluation
paragraphs: Apache Cassandra was another candidate I evaluated while looking for alternatives to SimpleDB.
As with the other replacements, it did not provide a compelling enough combination of simplicity, performance and cost for the Essential Skills workload.

sections.title: Repeated Replacement Testing
paragraphs: SimpleDB remained in production because I repeatedly tested alternatives rather than because the platform was unable to migrate.
DynamoDB, Aurora, RDS MySQL, Cassandra, Cosmos DB and Google Cloud options were all evaluated against the real operational requirements of the system.

sections.title: Python Data Tooling
paragraphs: Python became my primary language for cloud-data administration, migration and maintenance scripts.
Over the years I accumulated roughly 50 Python utilities that crawled, transformed, analyzed, backed up or migrated SimpleDB data.

sections.title: Weekly Backup Architecture
paragraphs: I created automated SimpleDB backup scripts that export production data approximately weekly into CSV files stored in S3.
Weekly scheduling kept backup costs controlled while still maintaining a practical recovery path.

sections.title: Simple Restore Model
paragraphs: SimpleDB was straightforward to restore because preserving the original item keys allowed records to be recreated directly without complex relational reconstruction.

sections.title: Vendor Exit & Disaster Recovery
paragraphs: Cloud portability was a deliberate architectural concern.

The Azure environment and Google Cloud research were designed to answer a concrete operational question: could Essential Skills continue operating if AWS became unavailable, unsuitable or commercially unacceptable?

sections.title: Architecture Principle
paragraphs: I chose databases based on measured operational fit rather than vendor recommendations or architectural fashion.

AWS teams regularly recommended newer services, but for this particular workload my testing repeatedly showed that SimpleDB delivered an unusually effective combination of speed, simplicity, low cost and automatic scaling.

historicalNotes: The legacy portfolio card was titled 'Amazon SDB' and contained only a brief statement about using SimpleDB for thousands of concurrent students.
The broader canonical card now represents Jamie's cloud-database architecture and migration work rather than SimpleDB alone.
The initial AWS/SimpleDB migration was driven by the goal of moving Hydra-Gen into WebStart/cloud operation around 2011.
SimpleDB became the primary production persistence layer for schools, teachers, students, classes, marks, assignments, login, usage, rostering, settings and related operational data.
At approximately 80,000 monthly users, Jamie remembers SimpleDB typically costing only about $20-$40 per month.
Jamie was the primary designer of the application's SimpleDB data model and optimization strategies.
Domains were intentionally treated similarly to relational tables despite AWS guidance encouraging less structured organization.
Jamie created application-level joins, bulk reads and correlation domains to avoid slow record-by-record cross-domain querying.
Large/BLOB-like payloads were stored in S3 with references from SimpleDB.
Jamie used batch operations where practical.
SmartDB/Rosetta served the Version 5 persistence generation.
Jamie created a new SimpleDB-focused persistence abstraction for Version 6 while preserving compatibility with the same production backend so Version 5 and Version 6 could coexist.
When Elastic Beanstalk deprecated PHP 5 and the SimpleDB SDK was no longer maintained for the newer environment, Jamie repaired/updated the SDK himself to keep production operating.
DynamoDB was used for Version 7 / Spelling List Editor, the ESS email-campaign system and supplementary non-critical services such as error reporting.
Aurora MySQL was intended as a serious migration path away from SimpleDB, not merely as an isolated Version 7 database.
Jamie adopted Aurora relatively early and later retired it because operational changes created disproportionate maintenance overhead.
Jamie evaluated RDS MySQL before Aurora.
MongoDB was used for lower-risk quote/internal-message data in the Customer Operations platform; authoritative school/student data remained in SimpleDB.
Do not include the hosted Mongo provider security incident in the public portfolio.
In 2018 Jamie cloned EC2 application workloads to Azure Virtual Machines and wrote Python tooling to migrate SimpleDB data into Azure Cosmos DB.

The migrated staging environment functioned in Azure but remained a disaster-recovery/vendor-exit fallback because Jamie found the Azure/Cosmos configuration slower and more expensive than the existing AWS/SimpleDB system.
Jamie also investigated Google Cloud around 2018 but did not complete a migration to the same level as Azure.
The likely Google NoSQL service explored was Cloud Datastore; exact historical service selection should be treated with medium confidence unless old scripts/configuration are recovered.
Apache Cassandra was also evaluated as a possible replacement.
Jamie repeatedly tested alternatives to SimpleDB; SimpleDB remained because it continued to perform unusually well for the actual workload.
Jamie has approximately 50 Python data-management scripts associated with crawling, transforming, backing up or migrating SimpleDB data.
SimpleDB data was backed up approximately weekly to CSV files stored in S3.
Restore was simplified by retaining original SimpleDB item keys.
Version 7 includes a working S3/JSON persistence mode partitioned hierarchically by school, teacher, student and custom-assignment data.
The S3/JSON persistence currently works alongside DynamoDB rather than only existing as a dormant alternative.
Cloud vendor-exit and disaster recovery were explicit architectural goals rather than hypothetical concerns.
